sections.title: The Interrogative Pronoun 哪
sections.body: When the interrogative pronoun 哪 is used in a question, the structure is 哪 plus a measure word or noun plus another noun. Examples include: 哪本书 (which book, where běn is a measure word for books), 哪个人 (which person, where gè is a general measure word), and 你是哪国人 (which country are you from).

sections.title: The Structural Particle 的 (de) for Possession
sections.body: The structure noun or pronoun plus 的 plus noun indicates possession or belonging. When the noun following 的 is a term of kinship (like 妈妈, 爸爸, 哥哥) or a noun that refers to a person (like 老师, 朋友, 同学), the 的 can be omitted.

sections.title: Numbers Below 100
sections.body: Chinese numbers from 1 to 99 follow a consistent pattern. The basic digits are: 1 yī, 2 èr, 3 sān, 4 sì, 5 wǔ, 6 liù, 7 qī, 8 bā, 9 jiǔ. Tens are formed by combining the digit with shí (10): 10 shí, 20 èrshí (two tens), 30 sānshí (three tens), and so on up to 90 jiǔshí (nine tens). Numbers between tens are formed by stating the tens place followed by the ones digit. For example, 19 is shíjiǔ (ten nine), 23 is èrshísān (two tens three), 56 is wǔshíliù (five tens six), 88 is bāshíbā (eight tens eight), and 99 is jiǔshíjiǔ (nine tens nine).

sections.title: Numbers Below 100
sections.body: Chinese numbers from 1 to 99 follow a consistent pattern. The basic digits are: 1 yī, 2 èr, 3 sān, 4 sì, 5 wǔ, 6 liù, 7 qī, 8 bā, 9 jiǔ. Tens are formed by combining the digit with shí (10): 10 shí, 20 èrshí (two tens), 30 sānshí (three tens), and so on up to 90 jiǔshí (nine tens). Numbers between tens are formed by stating the tens place followed by the ones digit. For example, 19 is shíjiǔ (ten nine), 23 is èrshísān (two tens three), 56 is wǔshíliù (five tens six), 88 is bāshíbā (eight tens eight), and 99 is jiǔshíjiǔ (nine tens nine).

sections.title: Numbers Below 100
sections.body: Chinese numbers from 1 to 99 follow a consistent pattern. The basic digits are: 1 yī, 2 èr, 3 sān, 4 sì, 5 wǔ, 6 liù, 7 qī, 8 bā, 9 jiǔ. Tens are formed by combining the digit with shí (10): 10 shí, 20 èrshí (two tens), 30 sānshí (three tens), and so on up to 90 jiǔshí (nine tens). Numbers between tens are formed by stating the tens place followed by the ones digit. For example, 19 is shíjiǔ (ten nine), 23 is èrshísān (two tens three), 56 is wǔshíliù (five tens six), 88 is bāshíbā (eight tens eight), and 99 is jiǔshíjiǔ (nine tens nine).

sections.title: Serial Verb Construction (1): 去 + place + to do something
sections.body: A serial verb construction has a predicate made up of two or more verbs in sequence. The second verb expresses the purpose of the first verb. The object of the first verb (the place) can sometimes be omitted. The basic pattern is: 去 (go) + place + action verb (what you do there).

rows: I go to China to study Chinese.
We go to a Chinese restaurant to eat Chinese food.
I go to school to read books.

sections.title: Serial Verb Construction (1): 去 + place + to do something
sections.body: A serial verb construction has a predicate made up of two or more verbs in sequence. The second verb expresses the purpose of the first verb. The object of the first verb (the place) can sometimes be omitted. The basic pattern is: 去 (go) + place + action verb (what you do there).

rows: I go to China to study Chinese.
We go to a Chinese restaurant to eat Chinese food.
I go to school to read books.

sections.title: The 有 Sentence: Indicating Existence
sections.body: The verb 有 can be used in an existential sentence to indicate that a person or thing exists in a particular location or place. The basic structure is: Location + 有 + Person/Thing.

rows: Under the chair there is a small dog
In the school there is a shop
On the table there is a computer and a book

sections.title: Negation of 有 Sentences
sections.body: The negative form of a 有 sentence uses 没有 instead of 有. When negating, do not use a numeral classifier before the object. For example: 椅子下面没有小狗 (There is no dog under the chair), 学校里没有商店 (There is no shop in the school), and 桌子上没有电脑和书 (There is no computer and book on the table).

sections.body: 在 is a verb that functions as the predicate of a sentence when followed by a word indicating location or direction. It is used to show where a person or thing is located.

sections.title: The Preposition 在
sections.body: 在 can act as a preposition, used before a word of locality to introduce the place where an action or behavior takes place. The structure is: Subject + 在 + Word of Locality + Verb.

sections.title: The 有 Sentence: Indicating Existence
sections.body: The verb 有 can be used in an existential sentence to indicate that a person or thing exists in a particular location or place. The basic structure is: Location + 有 + Person/Thing.

rows: Under the chair there is a small dog
In the school there is a shop
On the table there is a computer and a book

sections.title: Negation of 有 Sentences
sections.body: The negative form of a 有 sentence uses 没有 instead of 有. When negating, do not use a numeral classifier before the object. For example: 椅子下面没有小狗 (There is no dog under the chair), 学校里没有商店 (There is no shop in the school), and 桌子上没有电脑和书 (There is no computer and book on the table).

sections.title: The Conjunction 和
sections.body: The conjunction 和 is used to connect two or more elements in a parallel relationship. It links nouns, noun phrases, or other parallel structures together to show that they belong to the same category or are being discussed together.

rows: 我有一个中国朋友和一个美国朋友。
I have a Chinese friend and an American friend.

There are three people in my family: dad, mom, and me.

sections.title: Expression of Time with 点 and 分
sections.body: In Chinese, time is expressed using 点 (o'clock) for hours and 分 (minutes) for minutes, following the principle of larger units before smaller units. When expressing a whole hour, use 点 alone. When expressing minutes past the hour, use the pattern 点 + 分. Note that for 2 o'clock, always use 两点 (liǎng diǎn) rather than 二点 (èr diǎn). When minutes are less than ten, you can include 零 (líng, meaning zero) before the single digit minute.

sections.title: Distinguishing Morning and Afternoon
sections.body: To specify whether a time is in the morning or afternoon, add 上午 (morning) or 下午 (afternoon) before the time expression. The pattern is 上午/下午 + 点 + 分.

sections.title: The Noun 前 (Before/Prior To)
sections.body: The noun 前 can be used to refer to a period prior to the present time or the time being mentioned. It attaches to time expressions to indicate a deadline or time limit. Common examples include: 三天前 (three days ago or before three days), 一个星期前 (a week ago or before a week), 四点前 (before 4 o'clock), and 星期五前 (before Friday).

sections.title: Expression of Time with 点 and 分
sections.body: In Chinese, time is expressed using 点 (o'clock) for hours and 分 (minutes) for minutes, following the principle of larger units before smaller units. When expressing a whole hour, use 点 alone. When expressing minutes past the hour, use the pattern 点 + 分. Note that for 2 o'clock, always use 两点 (liǎng diǎn) rather than 二点 (èr diǎn). When minutes are less than ten, you can include 零 (líng, meaning zero) before the single digit minute.

sections.title: Distinguishing Morning and Afternoon
sections.body: To specify whether a time is in the morning or afternoon, add 上午 (morning) or 下午 (afternoon) before the time expression. The pattern is 上午/下午 + 点 + 分.

sections.body: In Chinese, a sentence can have a subject-predicate phrase as its predicate. The subject within the predicate phrase is usually part of or related to the main sentence subject.

sections.title: The Interjection 喂
sections.body: The word 喂 is commonly used when calling someone or answering a phone call. It serves as a greeting to get the other person's attention at the beginning of a telephone conversation.

rows: Hello, is Teacher Li at home?
She's not at home; she went to school.

sections.title: 在 and 呢 to Express Actions in Progress
sections.body: An action in progress can be expressed by adding the adverb 在 before a verb or by using the modal particle 呢 at the end of a sentence. You can use 在 alone, 呢 alone, or both together.

sections.title: Negative Form of Actions in Progress
sections.body: The negative form is 没在 or 没 plus a verb or verb phrase. Note that 呢 cannot be used at the end of negative sentences expressing actions in progress.
